7.14.m: kettle-drums, dundubhis, mṛdaṅgas, and kiṃkhara drums / were loudly sounded by thousands in both armies. / Then the hosts of gods, together with gandharvas and cāraṇas, / hearing the blast of musical instruments in the pramatha and asura armies, raised loud shouts. / By the sound of instruments from both armies and the roar of celestial lions, / lions, tigers, and elephants howled terribly on Mount Mandara. / With their prowess aroused by the rumbling sound of musical instruments, / the pramathas and asuras fought without breaking their own ranks. / At the first collision of those high-minded warriors in battle, / there was a dreadful roar like the trumpeting of elephants. / The gods and asuras, desirous of slaying each other, / excelled in the battle by means of weapons in their hands by the thousands. / With exceeding joy born of strong, excessive blows of spears, thunderbolts, stones, trees, and arrows, / the fight between the attendants and the asuras grew terribly dreadful, like the Tiṣya age. / Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-third chapter in the Skandapurāṇa, on the battle of the Gaṇas. / [Critical apparatus]

Then Virocana, the lord of the Daityas, like the radiant sun risen high,
entered the army of the pramathas, as the sun [enters] a mass of clouds. // 1
Mounting a four-tusked elephant adorned with tusks,

like the thousand-rayed [sun] blazing forth atop the eastern mountain. // 3

so did the heroic Virocana put the pramathas to flight. // 5

whichever pramatha the Asura caught sight of, that one he tore apart. // 6

7.14.m:
Just like bulls gazed upon by a lion, or like mortals beheld by Time,
the watching forces were gripped by terror when beheld and pursued by Vināyaka.
Wherever that god looked, lifting his hand like an elephant its trunk,
from there the Daitya army broke, as a blossoming forest before a tempest.
Seeing that army overwhelmed by the strong one, Bali's son, the foremost among the strong,
marched forth wishing to slay Vināyaka, like a rutted king of elephants against another rutted beast in battle.
As he rushed forward, blazing like the sun, furious as the sun-scorched Death in battle,
Kuṇḍodara advanced to check him and to fight in combat, like a lion facing another lion.
Both like lion cubs full of pride, or young tuskers with their trunks swinging wildly,
those two, intoxicated with the joy of battle, clashed: Kuṇḍodara and the son of Bali.
Drawing five hundred bows that resounded like a thunderbolt,
Bāṇa, roaring like a cloud, unleashed prime arrows at Kuṇḍodara.
At those sharp-pointed arrows of Bāṇa arriving then like enraged serpents,
Kuṇḍodara struck them all with a mountain-born [tree], as obstacles destroy desires.
Seeing those arrows lying fallen on the ground, rendered futile by the foe of the gods' enemies,
that enemy of the gods struck Kuṇḍodara with a spear, as Guha struck the lord of mountains, Krauñca, with his spear.
From the chest of the lord of Gaṇas, Bāṇa's spear drank blood,
as the wife of the thunderbolt-bearer drinks sweet, fragrant nectar brought by Śakra.

Held tight in the pair of Rāhu's arms, Vināyaka, garlanded with a thousand snakes,
thrashed, swinging the tip of his trunk, just like an elephant crossing the river of the gods.
Seeing Vināyaka whose movement was bound by Rāhu's arms, the sky-dwellers then,
the gods headed by Śakra, together with the yakṣas and the siddhas, cried out repeatedly, "Alas, alas!"
Then Kuṇḍodara, the foremost of yakṣas, revived like a crop watered with rain,
and taking an axe, struck Rāhu on the collarbone with his clenched fist.

7.14.m:
Hard-hit by that foremost yakṣa with the blow of the axe and with his fist,
Rāhu of terrible might released Vināyaka, as a noble man abandons an unrighteous deed.
Turning around like an elephant in rut dwelling in a forest thicket,
the elephant-faced god of terrifying trunk struck Rāhu with feet, tusks, and swinging trunk.
Battered by Vināyaka, Rāhu, that enemy of the gods, abandoned pride, arrogance, and strength,
and stood like a waterless cloud, or like a lord of elephants struck down by a lion.
While Rāhu was being tormented by Kuṇḍodara's fist-blows and by Vināyaka,
Kujambha, Saṃhrāda, Maya, together with Tāra, Huṇḍa, and Tuhuṇḍa then rushed at him.

Maya struck Kuṇḍodara with a trident, and Tāra struck him in the belly with a mace;
Bala struck him, who resembled a hanging cloud, with a fist like a thunderbolt;
and the son of Hiraṇyanetra's younger brother struck the terribly powerful Vināyaka with his palm.
His son also struck out of rage, and the mighty Tuhuṇḍa advanced as well.
Then seizing him, Vināyaka powerfully overpowered Tuhuṇḍa in battle with his trunk,
and dashing him down and tossing him up with terrible force, flung far away that [warrior] who was like an emissary of Yama.
Then striking Prahrāda, that god, alongside Maya whose chest was like dark collyrium,
uprooted [weapons] and roared a dreadful roar, like a cloud filled with bright water in the sky.
Kuṇḍodara too, the foremost of yakṣas, striking Bala, Tāra, and Kujambha,
[faced] both of those guardians of elephant-herds standing in battle, their garlands swaying, inflamed with fierce wrath.

Its overwhelming speed checked by the force of his arrows, hurled by the son of Śilāda with unfailing velocity, / struck by Kujambha, the thunderbolt turned back, just like a gift bestowed during a fit of madness.
Seeing that excellent thunderbolt obstructed, and hearing the roar let loose by Kujambha, / enraged, Nandī rushed toward that enemy, as Rāhu rushes at the sun in the vault of the sky.
Forcibly grasping the chariot by its pole-tip with his hand, the protector of the lord of pramathas / seized and hurled it away together with its charioteer and horses; and having hurled it, he roared terribly again.
Its front crushed, its horses disjointed, its charioteer, swords, headpieces, and rim-tips broken, / Kujambha's chariot fell from the vault of the sky, like a mountain whose wings were severed by the thunderbolt.
Leaping down from that chariot battered by the bull Nandi, the son of Prahrāda, undaunted in spirit, / seized a spear; undaunted in spirit, he stood firm like a thundering cloud flashing with lightning.
Licking his lips as though with a serpent's tongue, like Death hungry to devour, / blazing like a crest of the great fire, Jambha hurled it at Nandi.
Discharged by the arm of Indra's foe, that spear, fierce and intensely blazing like an Āṅgirasī sorcery, / was struck by the fire from Nandi's mouth and burned up like a moth in a flame.

Sanatkumāra said:
Seeing Kujambha slain by Nandī, who gladdens the gods, / the gods, cāraṇas, and great serpents raised a roar.
At that roar of the gods and at the death of Kujambha, / Jambha, the tiger among dānavas, gave way to immense rage.
From the limbs of that enraged demon, flames of fire burst forth, / like sparks scattering in every direction from Meru struck by a thunderbolt.
Resembling a cloud lit by meteors, Jambha, engulfed in fury, / ran forward to kill Nandī, as a king of lions runs toward an elephant.
Lifting up a terrible, massive iron mace weighing five hundred bhāras / forged of sharpened steel, the daitya ran toward Nandī:
“Halt now, wicked-natured one! Where will you go, now that I have seen you? / This iron mace, resembling the thunderbolt, shall crush you!”

(751)
Seeing the iron club seized forcibly by Śaṅkukarṇa, / the delighted gods shouted aloud and praised Śaṅkukarṇa. / The mighty Śaṅkukarṇa, fond of battle, having again seized the iron club, / roared, aimed at Jambha, and charged. / Then that tiger among Dānavas charged, eager for battle. / Then in the army of the lords of gaṇas, and likewise in the army of the Dānavas, / arose the sound of musical instruments mixed with lion-roars. / Then in the vault of the sky arose a noise resembling the roar of an agitated ocean or clouds, / as the denizens of heaven then watched that battle between the sons of Danu and the lords of the gaṇas. / The foremost among the Pramatha host together with the Nāgarudras, and the foremost Asuras together with Andhaka on the battlefield, / ceasing their fighting, stood watching the combat between the gaṇa-leader and the Dānava.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, on the battle of the gaṇas, in the Skandapurāṇa.

Sanatkumāra said:
Seeing Śaṅkukarṇa running towards Jambha, the mighty / Vṛtra ran towards him to slay him, like a lion against an elephant. / Śaṅkukarṇa too, the foremost among gaṇa-leaders, abandoning Jambha, / ran straight against Vṛtra, as lightning [strikes] a tree.

7.14.m:
As he rushed forward, Śaṃkukarṇa, the lord of the gaṇas, struck him with a tree, / with a śāla tree, and said, "Come here! Come here!"
Struck with the śāla tree by the enraged Śaṃkukarṇa, / the mighty Vṛtra approached and forcibly seized Śaṃkukarṇa by the foot.
Having seized Śaṃkukarṇa, Vṛtra whirled him around, helpless, / as a serpent might a bird, or as delusion, rising up, [whirls around] the world.
As Śaṃkukarṇa was whirled round on every side by Vṛtra, / thousands of ornaments fell shattered from his body.
Seeing him being whirled about by Vṛtra, all the gods / and lords of the gaṇas, crying "Alas, alas!" and bearing weapons and arrows, rushed forward to release him.
Seeing all those lords of the gaṇas approaching with sharp weapons in their hands, / Vṛtra released Śaṃkukarṇa in the assembly, as Garuḍa, king of birds, releases a serpent.

Sanatkumāra said: / Having whirled Śaṃkukarṇa round and cast him down upon the ground, / Vṛtra trampled the army of the pramathas, as an intoxicated elephant tramples a forest.
He struck Nandin, Nandiṣeṇa, and Somanandin, / put them to flight, and roared like a raincloud.
Then, as he was roaring, Viṭpati, best of Rudras, / shot an arrow like the thunderbolt-fire, bringing ruin to enemies.
Shot by Viṭpati, that arrow, brilliant as the rays of the sun, / entered Vṛtra, piercing him, as a perfected being enters a cloud in the sky.
Raising his own hand, like an elephant raising its trunk, that Danu's son / rushed at Viṭpati in the fight, as a wind rushes at a cloud.
With a trident the huge-bodied Nandī [struck] him, with a thunderbolt [struck] the dānava; / Somanandī struck with an axe, and Nandiṣeṇa with his palm.
And Viṭpati, exceedingly enraged, pierced Vṛtra in battle / with a thousand arrows, and again with twenty-one more.
Tormented by the leaders of the gaṇa-hosts, that dānava, huge as a mountain, / as he was being struck down, cried aloud like a tree inhabited by a deity.

Sprinkled with drops and sprays of blood from wounds, their white necklaces, ornaments, and garlands fallen, / with terror-stricken faces, those hosts of pramathas fled, severely tormented by the foes.
As towering white clouds in the sky, free of dust, [release] rain of fresh water, / so the sons of Diti released an overwhelming rain of arrows, terrifying in its immense velocity.
Then, resembling elephants, mountains, and clouds, possessing splendor equal to fire and the sun, / unleashing a vast mesh of pure, sharp arrows, the principal daityas struck the pramatha hosts.
Then, with [weapons] resembling iron clubs, arrows, and swords, discharged from hundreds of prime mechanical contrivances in their hands, / the gaṇas, inspiring fear in the foes of the thirty [gods], marched forth, engaging in battle.
Excellent elephants resembling mountain peaks, swift-running [steeds], and numerous choice horses, / and terrifying chariots like the abodes of the gods fell shattered and consumed at the front of battle.
Firmly gouged by arrowheads, their fine garments soaked with blood from wounds, / their eyes rolling, their life-breath and vital strength departed, Danu's sons were crushed by the hundreds.
With fallen, excellent white necklaces, earrings, diadems, crowns, jewels, garlands, and garments, / the ground at the front of battle shone radiant like Urvaśī adorned with splendid, choice jewels.

7.14.m:
Yama, Varuṇa, the lord of wealth, and Vāsava, / the Bhagas, the Vasus, the sun, the moon, and the wind gods, / with delighted eyes and lotus faces, furious in crushing the host of enemies, held them back.
With mighty elephants roaming like rain clouds and winds rushing like galloping horses, / turbid with lightning strikes of arrows, the stormy gloom at the end of battle did not cease.
With eyes resembling lotus petals, faces shining like lotuses, the sun, and the moon, / the excellent faces of the sons of Danu made the earth shine forth as though covered with lotuses.
With the lords of the gaṇas and Dānavas crushed, smeared with the sprinkling of blood, fat, and marrow, / the battle was exceedingly terrible, dreadful, and watched by flocks of Garuḍas and Piśācas.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-first chapter in the Skandapurāṇa, in the battle of the gaṇas.

7.14.m:
Sanatkumāra said:
While that battle was raging between the armies of the pramathas and the asuras, / the sound of bows was heard like clouds in the rainy season,
and the roar of mighty elephants, the neighing of horses, / and the cries of the gods and rakṣasas engrossed in the battle-gāndharva,
harsh to the ears, dreadful like the crash of a thunderbolt. / They are heard and indeed swell like the debts of debtors.
Then a Dānava named Kārtasvana, sounding like a cloud, / struck down the pramathas in battle like Death approaching mortals.
Mounted on his chariot, wielding a bow, holding arrows, armored, and wearing earrings, / he burned the army of the pramathas like fire burns dry grass.

7.14.m:
Showers of arrows fell upon the army of the gaṇas as if upon a mountain.
With the sound of musical instruments silenced, terrified by the impact of arrows, / the army of the gaṇa-lords became red like a forest of bandhujīva flowers.
Just as wind scatters clouds, as Garuḍa scatters serpents, / as a tiger scatters spotted deer, as the sun dispels masses of darkness,
so the enraged Kārtasvana, with exceedingly dreadful thunderbolt-like arrows, / burned the commanders of the gaṇas like the fire of cosmic dissolution burns the worlds.
Seeing the army of the gaṇa-lords burned, consumed, and afflicted with pain, / the enraged god Viṭpati then spoke to Kārtasvana.
Standing firm against the fall of arrows, Rudra of rudra-like valor, / being enraged, drew an arrow from his quiver against the Dānava chief:

Then, having pulled out that very arrow shot by the Dānava, / Viṭpati hurled it at Kārtasvana and roared aloud.
That arrow released by Viṭpati, bringing destruction to Dānavas, / carried off the head of the Dānava’s charioteer ten arrow-lengths away.
When his charioteer was killed, his swift and dappled horses in battle / ran amok, carrying off the chariot like hawks seizing meat.
“Kārtasvana’s chariot is fleeing! Why do you sit idle? Seize it!” / Thus arose a great uproar among the chiefs of the Dānavas.
That best of chariots, wandering across the vast slope of Mount Mandara, / shone like the sun's excellent chariot drawn by seven horses wandering upon Mount Meru.
Then, leaping down from that excellent chariot with swift horses, / bow in hand, Kārtasvana rushed toward Viṭpati.
Then a roar of "Well done! Well done!" arose from both armies, / as Kārtasvana wished to fight once more with Viṭpati.

Having cut down those arrows, with a thousand feathered shafts / that consume life-breath, he pierced Kārtasvana and roared.
With those arrows whose heads appeared at his back, the dānava shone / like a mountain with excellent serpents half-emerged from fissures.
Then the enraged Rudra cut down his bow, sword, / and the quivers into five parts; and the powerful one tormented him.
Then Viṭpati, having noble might, loosed a straight-flying arrow, / equal to Indra's thunderbolt, raging like a hissing lord of serpents, afflicting the son of Diti.
That king of arrows, shot by the excellent Rudra, emitting a trail of smoke on the battlefield, / forcibly severed the face of the asura in battle, just as a noble-minded sage plucks a lotus.
Then an uproar was raised with dread roars by the deities, / the best sages, and the pramathas, / seeing the enemy's head taken off in battle by the subduer of the fire of the mare's mouth.

760 / Sanatkumāra said: / Having killed his enemy Kārtasvana with a great golden shaft, / Viṭpati burned the daityas as fire burns moths.
With drawn bow, the god, wearing handsome golden earrings, / roared, discharging arrows among the dānavas like the sun releasing rays.
Equipped with golden feathers made of Garuḍa's plumage, / those arrows fell upon the dānavas like misfortunes sent by fate.
With severed faces, severed hands, severed feet, bellies, and thighs, / dānavas fell by the hundreds upon the earth like mountains.

7.14.m:
Somanandin, Nandin, the attendant Nandiṣeṇa, / Prabhāmaya, Vīrabhadra, Sūryāpyāyana, / Pañcākṣa, Kopapāla, Trinetra, Piṅgalekṣaṇa, / Rākṣasa, Piṅgala, who roars from his abode in the cremation grounds, / Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Śaṅkukarṇa, the mighty Kuṇḍodara, / Airāvatamukha, Annapāla, Kapāladhṛk, / and Vināyaka himself with his long, stout trunk— / these and other gaṇa leaders, called forth in the hundreds by the hosts, / entered to burn the Dānavas, as fires burn dry trees. / Surrounding Viṭpati, all roaring like young lordly elephants, / with tridents, discus-weapons, arrows, and bhuśuṇḍi guns in hand, the leaders of the gaṇas, minded for battle, advanced. / Then between them there arose close combat, fierce in battle, / like that of rut-maddened bull elephants gathered with cow elephants in the forests. / Beholding that great battle of the Dānavas with the gaṇa leaders, the gods / moved through the sky in celestial aerial chariots, uttering lion-roars and clapping their hands.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-third chapter in the Skandapurāṇa, on the battle of the gaṇas.

Naigameṣa, born of Agni, fought Hayagrīva and Sugrīva, / the lords of the Dānavas, as the slayer of Madhu fought Madhu. / Jambha fought with Nandin, Tuhuṇḍa with Somanandin, / and the Dānava Huṇḍa fought the heroic Vināyaka.
Mahākāya fought with Kāla, Namuci with Ghana, / and Ilvaka and Pilvaka with the two Piṅgala gaṇa leaders. / Hrāda clashed with Śaṅkukarṇa, and Viṭpati with Anuhrāda; / the Rudra Ādityāpyāyana met with Saṃhrāda. / Kuṇḍodara, the lord of Yakṣas, and the attendant Ghaṇṭākarṇa / clashed with Bala and Ilvala, like two lions with two elephants. / Bali clashed with Pañcākṣa, a Rudra resplendent as the sun, / and the Dānava who fathered Bali fought with Vīrabhadra.

7.14.m:
Sticking in Vināyaka's chest, that spear shone
like a streak of gold on a sapphire gem. / 22
Drawing out Huṇḍa's spear, which was like a sunbeam, with the tip of his trunk, the god
suddenly slew Huṇḍa with that very [spear], as his younger brother [slew] Mount Krauñca. / 23
Seeing Tuhuṇḍa and Huṇḍa destroyed by Vināyaka, the destroyer of foes,
the entire army of the leaders of the gaṇas became like the frenzied Gaṅgā. / 24
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fourth chapter in the Skandapurāṇa, in the battle of the gaṇas.
